clue.text: His real character in Flemish guise

indicators.note: a guise is a new outward form, so the letters of the word before it are dressed up in a new order

explanation.surface: A Flemish disguise covers up a man's true nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ... guise' signals the anagram: FLEMISH rearranged; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: When a person is truly being their own self, it is their genuine nature on show, hence 'his real character'.

clue.text: Ready to take offence over draughts?

definitions.text: Ready to take offence over draughts?

parts.words: Ready to take offence over draughts?
parts.note: in the board game draughts a player may 'huff' an opponent's piece, while a touchy person is quick to take a huff

explanation.definitionFit: Someone quick to sulk or bristle is prone to take a huff, petulant and easily offended.

clue.text: Soldier she went out with?

parts.note: a woman's date who is a soldier could be called her armed companion, though the phrase really means a guard of troops

explanation.definitionFit: A detachment of troops accompanying a person or convoy for protection is the real sense; the clue pictures a soldier boyfriend.

clue.text: Legendary Norse poems by a theologian in each case

indicators.note: the theologian's letters are placed inside the casing formed from the abbreviation for each

parts.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each, here serving as the case
DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a theologian

explanation.surface: A theologian's book of old Scandinavian verse, cited for every instance.
explanation.walkthrough: DD (Doctor of Divinity) goes inside EA, the abbreviation for 'each'; 'by a' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Icelandic collections of Old Norse mythological and heroic verse are known by this name.

clue.text: More forward college student

definitions.meaning: ... as a comparative means cheekier, more impudent
a first-year student at a British university or college

explanation.definitionFit: Cheekier or more impertinent is one sense; a first-year undergraduate in British usage is the other.

clue.text: Kill, kill! But it's already dead

parts.note: to do someone in is to kill them; slang 'do' means kill
'do' again, slang for kill

explanation.surface: A frenzied cry to kill something that has in fact already died.
explanation.walkthrough: The extinct bird is the thing already dead.
explanation.definitionFit: The flightless Mauritian bird was hunted to extinction, the classic example of something long gone.

clue.text: Bids to break up and cease to function

indicators.note: breaking up the word bids means its letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Offers for a business collapse and it shuts down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to break up' signals the anagram of BIDS, giving DISB; add AND.
explanation.definitionFit: An organisation that breaks up its members and stops operating has dissolved itself.

clue.text: Performs with animals

definitions.meaning: carries out, as in 'she ... her duty'
female deer or rabbits are so called

explanation.definitionFit: Third person of 'do' gives 'performs'; the plural of a female deer gives the animals.

clue.text: State of being powerless to resist

definitions.text: State of being powerless to resist

parts.words: State of being powerless to resist
parts.note: describes torpor or sluggishness, but also the physics property of a body that keeps doing what it was doing

explanation.definitionFit: Inactivity, lethargy, a reluctance to move or change, which leaves one unable to act against things.

clue.text: Given by one considering taking up nursing?

definitions.text: Given by one considering taking up nursing?

parts.words: Given by one considering taking up nursing?
parts.note: someone pondering a career in nursing gives thought to care, and that thought is full of care

explanation.definitionFit: Deliberation full of attention and caution is what a careful thinker gives a matter.

clue.text: Discussion for which tails are obligatory?

definitions.text: Discussion for which tails are obligatory?

parts.words: Discussion for which tails are obligatory?
parts.note: pictures a debate where tailcoats must be worn, though the phrase means a major parliamentary debate

explanation.definitionFit: A formal parliamentary debate on an important matter, attended in force, is called this; formal dress means tails.

clue.text: One turning to a Greek letter

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one

indicators.note: turning the little word to means reading it backwards

explanation.surface: Someone converting to a Greek letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' is the reversal signal and acts only on 'to'; 'One' is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, the smallest, hence also 'a tiny amount'.

clue.text: Little squeaker to quieten with grain

parts.note: 'sh!' is said to quieten someone
oats are a cereal grain

explanation.surface: Feeding a small noisy creature some grain to keep it quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: A squeaker is a young animal that squeals, here a piglet.
explanation.definitionFit: A young pig just weaned, and piglets squeal, so a little squeaker.

clue.text: Pummel and hide

definitions.meaning: to strike repeatedly with missiles or blows
an animal's skin with the fur on

explanation.definitionFit: To bombard with blows is one sense; an animal skin is the other.

clue.text: Major opposition

parts.note: reads as big resistance, but asks for the word that is the opposite of major

explanation.definitionFit: Lesser or junior is the antonym of greater or senior, so it stands opposed to major.

clue.text: Cooking a batch of cakes, say, a Lancashire town

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken, its sound giving the town's spelling

parts.note: to bake up is to cook a batch of something

explanation.surface: Baking a tray of cakes in a northern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: BACUP is a small mill town in Lancashire, a county in northern England; it is pronounced like 'bake up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in the Rossendale valley of north-west England.

clue.text: One who runs with the hare and hounds

definitions.text: One who runs with the hare and hounds

parts.words: One who runs with the hare and hounds
parts.note: hare and hounds is a paper-chase game, so its runner is a cross-country athlete, also a hunting dog for hares

explanation.definitionFit: A cross-country runner, a member of a running club, and also a hound bred for hunting hares.

clue.text: Count batty in a novel way

definitions.text: Count batty in a novel way

parts.words: Count batty in a novel way
parts.note: a count who turns into a bat in a famous book; 'batty' looks like 'crazy'

explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker's vampire nobleman, who changes into a bat in his 1897 novel.

clue.text: Do nothing when arranging a country dance

indicators.note: arranging the letters puts them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
O, a zero, means nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: Being idle while organising a dance in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when arranging' signals the anagram of DO, O and WHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A lively American folk gathering with square dancing is called this.

clue.text: Percy from Tottenham?

parts.note: Sir Henry Percy's nickname is also the name of the Tottenham football club

explanation.walkthrough: Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club; Harry Percy, in Shakespeare's Henry IV, bore the same nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Nickname of Sir Henry Percy, the medieval rebel, which the north London football club took.

clue.text: Made ineffective sharpshooter carried in case of need

indicators.note: carried in the case formed by the following word means placed inside it

parts.note: taken as written
a gat is slang for a gun, something that shoots

explanation.surface: A marksman's gun was carried just in case and so was rendered useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sharpshooter' looks like a marksman but is a gun, gangster slang; 'carried in case of' puts it inside the word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To render something null or void, cancelling its effect, is to nullify it.

clue.text: Hut soon demolished in Texas

indicators.note: demolishing the words knocks their letters down and rebuilds them differently

explanation.surface: A hut is soon knocked down in the Lone Star state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demolished' signals the anagram of HUT SOON.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest city of the state of Texas is found there.

clue.text: The pale mixture left in a glass of liquor

definitions.text: left in a glass of liquor

indicators.note: a mixture of the words means their letters stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A pale cocktail remains at the bottom of a drinking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixture' signals the anagram of THE PALE.
explanation.definitionFit: The dregs of drink remaining at the bottom of a glass after drinking.

clue.text: Way connected with spirit

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Way connected with spirit', gives RUM for spirit but nothing builds NOST and no definition is left; likely OCR loss of a word (e.g. 'No').

clue.text: Small bloodsucker not without credit

definitions.meaning: a tiny parasitic arachnid that feeds on blood

explanation.definitionFit: A blood-sucking mite-like parasite is one sense; British slang for credit, as in 'buying on tick', is the other.

clue.text: Initially no right to express sorrow for a bird

indicators.note: no right initially: the first-placed R is dropped from the front of the word

parts.note: to regret is to express sorrow

explanation.surface: With no right to regret anything at first, sorrow over a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially no' removes the R from the front of REGRET.
explanation.definitionFit: A white heron of marshes and shores is this wading bird.

clue.text: Talent that's negative to ourselves

parts.note: no is the negative reply
us refers to ourselves

explanation.surface: A gift that brings refusal to the speakers.
explanation.walkthrough: NOUS is British informal for common sense or know-how.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal for practical intelligence or know-how, a natural aptitude.

clue.text: Plain, for example, Virginia

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Plain, for example, Virginia', has EG inside VA but no container indicator; a word may be missing from the OCR, and no source found.

clue.text: One against German agreement about an island

parts.note: ja is German for yes

indicators.note: about means turned round, so these two short pieces are read backwards

parts.note: a means one
v, versus, means against

explanation.surface: One person opposes a German deal about an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses A and V to give VA, after JA.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia's most populous island, home to Jakarta.

clue.text: Faultless apparently, but you don't know him

definitions.text: Faultless apparently, but you don't know him

parts.words: Faultless apparently, but you don't know him
parts.note: a flawless foreigner on the surface, but the phrase means someone utterly unknown to you

explanation.definitionFit: A person completely unfamiliar to one, 'perfect' meaning complete rather than flawless.

clue.text: Archbishop to admire

definitions.meaning: William ... was Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I

explanation.definitionFit: The 17th-century Archbishop of Canterbury executed in 1645 is one sense; to extol is the other.

clue.text: Sounds a cooler cat, albeit immaterial

indicators.note: sounds says the phrase is heard, and its sound is spelt differently

parts.note: a fan is a cooler, and a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A trendier cat that is strangely not quite there.
explanation.walkthrough: FAN + TOM, said aloud, is the ghostly adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghostly or illusory, having no physical substance.
